questions.q: **REMEMBER:** Define a "Budget" as a single-use plan. State its two primary functions in an organisation.
questions.a:
A Budget is a single-use plan that is a statement of expected results expressed in numerical terms for a specific period. Its two primary functions are: (1) **Planning** — it quantifies future facts and figures (revenues, expenses, resource needs) forcing managers to think ahead; (2) **Control** — it provides standards (expected figures) against which actual performance is compared, so deviations can be detected and corrected.  
**Wrong answer reveals:** If the student says "Budget is just a financial statement" or "Budget only controls costs," they confuse the *plan* (future-oriented) with the *financial statement* (past-oriented) and miss the dual planning-control role that NCERT explicitly highlights.

questions.q: **UNDERSTAND:** A company prepares a "Sales Budget" forecasting ₹5 crore revenue for Q1. At the end of Q1, actual revenue is ₹4.2 crore. The marketing manager says, "The budget failed, so budgets are useless." Using the NCERT concept of Budget as a control device, explain why the manager's conclusion is flawed.
questions.a:
The manager confuses *accuracy of forecast* with *utility of budget*. NCERT states: "Since budget represents all items in numbers, it becomes easier to compare actual figures with expected figures and take corrective action subsequently. Thus, a budget is also a control device from which deviations can be taken care of." The ₹80 lakh shortfall is not a failure of the budget; it is the **variance** that the budget *revealed*. Without the budget, the shortfall might have gone unnoticed until cash flow crashed. The budget did its job: it set a standard (₹5 cr), exposed the deviation (-₹80L), and now enables corrective action (e.g., push promotions, revise Q2 targets).  
**Wrong answer reveals:** If the student agrees with the manager, they view budgets as *predictions that must come true* rather than *benchmarks for control*. This is a classic board-exam trap: "Budget failed → planning is useless" ignores the controlling function entirely.

questions.q: **APPLY:** "GreenEarth Ltd." plans to launch a new organic tea brand. This is a one-time project. Draft the **three core components** of the single-use plan for this launch, specifying one concrete element that must appear in each component (Programme, Budget, Schedule). Use Indian context (₹, months, etc.).
questions.a:
**Programme:** Objective — "Achieve 5% market share in Delhi-NCR organic tea segment within 6 months." Policies — "Only eco-friendly packaging." Procedures — "Distributor onboarding: 3-step verification." Rules — "No plastic in secondary packaging." Resources — "Hire 10 sales executives, lease 2 delivery vans."  
**Budget (₹):** Expected Revenue — ₹1.2 cr (Year 1); Expected Expenses — ₹95 lakh (Production ₹40L, Marketing ₹30L, Distribution ₹15L, Admin ₹10L); Expected Surplus — ₹25 lakh.  
**Schedule (Timeline):** Month 1 — Finalise recipe & packaging design; Month 2 — FSSAI licence & vendor contracts; Month 3 — Production trial run & distributor appointments; Month 4 — Marketing campaign launch; Month 5 — Distribution to 200 retail outlets; Month 6 — Review sales vs. budget.  
**Wrong answer reveals:** If the student lists only tasks without linking them to the three distinct documents (e.g., writes a mixed to-do list), they haven't grasped that Programme, Budget, and Schedule are *separate, formal documents* each serving a distinct purpose (what/how, how much, when).

questions.q: **ANALYZE:** Compare a **Programme** and a **Schedule** in terms of (a) scope of detail, (b) primary focus, and (c) relationship to the Budget. Use a table or structured points.
questions.a:
| Aspect | Programme | Schedule |
|--------|-----------|----------|
| **Scope of detail** | Broad & comprehensive: covers objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, **human & physical resources**, **and the budget itself**. | Narrow & time-focused: only the **sequence, duration, start/end dates, and dependencies** of tasks. |
| **Primary focus** | **What** needs to be done and **how** (the complete course of action). | **When** each task must start/finish to meet the deadline. |
| **Relationship to Budget** | The Programme **includes** the Budget as one of its components ("the budget to implement any course of action"). | The Schedule **operationalises** the Budget's time dimension: Budget says "₹30L marketing in Year 1"; Schedule says "₹5L in Month 1, ₹8L in Month 2…" enabling cash-flow planning. |
**Wrong answer reveals:** If the student says "Programme is just a big schedule" or "Schedule includes the budget," they conflate the *strategic blueprint* (Programme) with the *tactical timetable* (Schedule). NCERT: "Programmes are detailed statements… which outlines the objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, human and physical resources required **and the budget**." The Schedule is not mentioned as a component of the Programme in NCERT; it is a separate single-use plan.

questions.q: **EVALUATE:** "Budgets are only for the finance department; operational managers (production, sales, HR) don't need to understand them." Critique this statement using the NCERT concept of Budget as a **fundamental planning instrument** and **control device** for *all* departments.
questions.a:
The statement is **false and dangerous**. NCERT: "It is a fundamental planning instrument in many organisations." A **Production Budget** (units to produce, raw material needed) is useless if the Production Manager doesn't understand it; a **Sales Budget** (territory-wise targets) guides the Sales Manager's daily decisions; a **Cash Budget** (inflows/outflows) requires input from *every* department (sales collections, purchase payments, salary payouts). As a control device, budgets let *each* department head compare "Actual vs. Budget" for their area (e.g., "My department spent ₹12L vs budget ₹10L → investigate"). If only Finance understands budgets, (a) departmental plans become unrealistic (Finance doesn't know machine capacity), (b) variances are detected late, (c) no ownership → no corrective action.  
**Wrong answer reveals:** If the student agrees, they treat Budget as a *financial accounting report* rather than a *managerial planning-control tool* permeating all functions. This misconception costs marks in case-study questions where a department head must act on a budget variance.

questions.q: **CREATE:** Design a **single-use plan outline** for a new situation: "A government hospital setting up a 50-bedded COVID-19 isolation ward in 3 weeks." Provide: (a) 2 Objectives for the Programme, (b) 3 line-items for the Budget (with estimated ₹), (c) 4 milestones with dates for the Schedule. Ensure the three components are consistent (e.g., Budget covers resources needed for Schedule milestones).
questions.a:
**Programme Objectives:**  
1. Operationalise 50 oxygen-supported isolation beds with ICU backup by **Day 21**.  
2. Train 100% deployed staff (doctors, nurses, sanitation) on COVID protocols by **Day 14**.  

**Budget (Estimated ₹):**  
1. Medical Equipment (50 oxygen concentrators, 10 ventilators, monitors) — **₹1.2 crore**  
2. Consumables (PPE kits, medicines, oxygen cylinders for 30 days) — **₹45 lakh**  
3. Human Resource (incentive pay for 40 extra nurses & 10 doctors for 30 days) — **₹60 lakh**  
**Total Estimated Budget: ₹2.25 crore**  

**Schedule (Milestones):**  
| Milestone | Target Date | Depends on Budget Line |
|-----------|-------------|------------------------|
| 1. Tender & Procurement of Equipment | Day 3 | Line 1 (₹1.2 cr) |
| 2. Electrical/Oxygen pipeline civil work | Day 7 | Line 1 (part) |
| 3. Staff Recruitment & Training Completion | Day 14 | Line 3 (₹60 lakh) |
| 4. Ward Commissioning & Mock Drill | Day 21 | All lines |

**Consistency check:** Budget Line 1 funds Milestones 1 & 2; Line 3 funds Milestone 3; all lines converge at Milestone 4.  
**Wrong answer reveals:** If the student's Budget items don't map to Schedule milestones (e.g., budgets for "furniture" but Schedule has "ventilator installation"), they treat the three components as independent silos. The essence of a single-use plan is **integration** — Programme defines *what*, Budget quantifies *how much*, Schedule sequences *when*; they must reference the same resources and timeline.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Single-use plans are specific, one-time plans designed for a unique, non-recurring event or project (e.g., launching a new product, ______ a conference, opening a new branch).
Fill in the blank: Imagine your school is hosting an inter-school science fest for the first time — a one-time, non-______ event.
What is Single-use plans? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Single-use plans are specific, one-time plans designed for a unique, non-recurring event or project (e.g., launching a new product, organizing a conference, opening a new branch).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Single-use plans?
questions.a: Misconception: "A Programme, a Budget, and a Schedule are just three names for the same project plan document." Why students make this error: In everyday language, we say "Here's the plan for the event" meaning one document.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) distinguish between a Programme, a Budget, and a Schedule with a concrete example for each, and (2) explain how a Budget functions as both a planning tool (quantifying the future) and a controlling tool (comparing actual vs. expected figures to trigger corrective action).
